# Results — Study 45 (Vanishing-Act): the size premium across the longest free proxies

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). Monthly returns of three size pairs
(Yahoo): **^RUT − ^GSPC** (Russell 2000 vs S&P 500, 1987–2026 — the long history, **price indices**:
no dividends on either leg, and since large caps yield more, a total-return spread would be *more*
negative — conservative in the premium's favour) and the total-return ETF pairs **IWM − SPY** and
**IJR − IVV** (2000–2026). SMB = small − large; leg Sharpes are computed on each pair's **common
months only**. As-of **2026-06-01** (complete months only); inputs fingerprint `21b43ddb5825`.*

## The verdict, earned — Signal `NONE` · Tradability `MIRAGE` · "Survived publication"? `BUSTED`

The size premium is finance's original factor (Banz 1981) — and on the longest free proxy it simply
**isn't there**. Russell 2000 minus S&P 500 over **39 years** earns **+0.03%/yr at a Sharpe of 0.00
(Lo t = 0.02)** — zero to two decimal places — and on the same months small-caps **trail** large-caps
risk-adjusted (Sharpe 0.47 vs 0.62). The tradable ETF spreads are statistically insignificant too (Lo
t 0.5–1.0). And note what this sample *is*: Banz published in 1981, the data starts in 1987 — **every
month here is post-publication**. There is no "worked, then died" story to tell on this bench; the
honest reading is harsher: across 39 post-publication years a positive premium never showed up, and
the sign of any "10-year size premium" is a window choice (the trailing decade's mean swings from
**−5.0%** to **+6.9%**/yr and is positive in only 56% of windows). The factor that defined the
small-cap fund industry did not survive its own publication — `BUSTED`.

## Data stamp

- **Long history**: ^RUT − ^GSPC (price indices), 1987-10 → 2026-05, 464 months
- **Tradable**: IWM − SPY and IJR − IVV total return, 2000-06 → 2026-05, 312 months
- As-of 2026-06-01, fingerprint `21b43ddb5825`

## The premium is statistically zero — and small-caps lose on Sharpe

| pair | period (common months) | SMB mean/yr | SMB Sharpe | Lo t | small Sharpe | large Sharpe |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ^RUT − ^GSPC | 1987-10..2026-05 (464) | **+0.03%** | **0.00** | **0.02** | 0.47 | 0.62 |
| IWM − SPY | 2000-06..2026-05 (312) | +0.91% | 0.09 | 0.46 | 0.51 | 0.61 |
| IJR − IVV | 2000-06..2026-05 (312) | +1.93% | 0.19 | 0.96 | 0.58 | 0.61 |

Not one pair clears |t| = 2. On the longest series the spread is *zero*, and small-caps deliver a
*lower* Sharpe than large-caps **on the same months** — the opposite of a risk-adjusted premium.
(Both legs of every comparison share one sample by construction; comparing a 1993-start SPY to a
2000-start IWM would smuggle the late-90s run-up into one leg only.) The S&P 600 pair (IJR, which
screens constituents for profitability) does marginally best, hinting the surviving "size" edge is
really a **quality screen**, not size.

## The "turn in 2010" is a window choice, not a decay event

| window split at 2010 (post-hoc) | pre-2010 mean/yr | 2010-on mean/yr | difference | block-bootstrap p |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ^RUT − ^GSPC | +1.1% | −1.4% | +2.6% | **0.45** |
| IWM − SPY | +5.7% | −1.9% | +7.7% | 0.03 |
| IJR − IVV | +7.7% | −1.4% | +9.1% | 0.02 |

Two honest observations, in order. First, this **cannot be a post-publication decay test**: Banz
published in 1981 and the earliest data here is 1987 — the "pre" window is as post-publication as the
"post". Second, on the only long series the celebrated turn **dissolves under a real test**: pre-2010
SMB was +1.1%/yr at a Sharpe of 0.09 (itself indistinguishable from zero), and the pre/post difference
carries a block-bootstrap p of 0.45 — pure window noise. The ETF pairs' 2000s-vs-2010s gap is
detectable (p ≈ 0.02–0.03), but both start in 2000: what it shows is that small-caps had one good
decade (2000s, after the dot-com bust deflated mega-cap large) and one bad one — **regime dependence,
not a publication event**. The trailing-10-year exhibit makes the same point without any split: the
"size premium" has flipped sign repeatedly for four decades.

## The honest takeaway

The size premium — the factor that launched a thousand small-cap funds — is a `MIRAGE` today and, on
this bench, was never measurably there: zero over 39 post-publication years, small-caps trailing
large on Sharpe on identical samples, and a sign that depends on which decade you ask. What little
edge survives in the S&P 600 pair looks like a quality screen wearing a size label (Asness et al.
2018). `NONE` on the spread, `MIRAGE` to trade, and the survived-publication claim `BUSTED` — not
because the premium faded after the paper, but because four decades of post-paper data never showed
it at all.
